subject: brain
topic: Social hierarchies can physically alter the neurochemistry of your brain
angle: While the amygdala specifically codes for social rank and its neural structure relates to social hierarchy knowledge, there is no evidence in these sources that social status directly alters dopamine receptor sensitivity.
title: The Neurochemistry of Status

hooks.text: Is your social status written in your brain?
You think status is a feeling. Your brain treats it as a map.
You are physically mapping the hierarchy of your workplace.
A chair at the head of a long table.
The brain codes for social rank.

reveal.headline: Your brain maps social rank.
reveal.body: The amygdala expresses a neural signal that codes for social rank and predicts how you make investment decisions.

explain.headline: Structure shapes your neural map.
explain.body: Neural activity in the amygdala is linked to the development of knowledge about social hierarchies. Variations in amygdala gray matter volume are linked to how you perform on social transitivity.

matters.headline: The hierarchy is physical.
matters.body: That may be why your perception of status is not just a thought. It is a structural part of your brain's knowledge.

example.headline: A quiet office.
example.body: You sit in a meeting room and notice who speaks first. You instinctively know who holds the power and how to react to them.

stat.label: the neural signal that predicts investment decisions

claims.text: Structural variations in amygdala gray matter volume are linked to interindividual differences in social transitivity performance.
claims.quote: Further, structural variations in amygdala gray matter volume accounted for interindividual differences in social transitivity performance.

claims.text: The amygdala expressed a neural signal selectively coding for social rank, which predicted the influence of rank on participants' investment decisions.
claims.quote: Finally, the amygdala expressed a neural signal selectively coding for social rank, whose robustness predicted the influence of rank on participants' investment decisions.

claims.text: Neural activity in the amygdala is linked to the development of knowledge about social hierarchies, but not nonsocial hierarchies.
claims.quote: We found that neural activity in the amygdala tracked the development of knowledge about a social, but not a nonsocial, hierarchy.

claims.text: The ABC intervention improves biological regulation by making children receiving it show more typical cortisol production, with higher wake-up cortisol values and a steeper diurnal slope.
claims.quote: Following the intervention, children receiving the ABC intervention (n = 49) showed more typical cortisol production, with higher wake-up cortisol values and a steeper diurnal slope, than children receiving the control intervention (n = 51).

claims.text: Emotion-induction procedures are associated with increases in cortisol that may subsequently return to equilibrium regardless of emotion-regulation instructions.
claims.quote: Taken together, the findings indicate that emotion-induction procedures are associated with increases in cortisol that may subsequently return to equilibrium regardless of emotion-regulation instructions.

claims.text: The linear structure of both social and nonsocial hierarchies is represented at a neural level in the hippocampus.
claims.quote: In contrast, we observed that the linear structure of both social and nonsocial hierarchies was represented at a neural level in the hippocampus.

verdict: The sources show that the brain has specific regions for processing social rank and that certain interventions can regulate cortisol, but they do not link social status to dopamine receptor changes.
caveat: The sources do not provide any data on dopamine receptor sensitivity or the direct causal link between social status and neurochemistry.
caption:
Social hierarchies are not just abstract concepts. They are processed by specific regions of your brain. 

Research shows the amygdala codes for social rank and influences investment decisions, though there is no evidence that status directly alters dopamine receptor sensitivity. 

How does your environment shape your brain's map?
